question.value: Provide accurate rotational frequencies of n- and i-butanal in the millimeter-wave region, search for them toward Sgr B2(N) and G+0.693-0.027, and test the level of complexity that interstellar chemistry can reach in star-forming regions.

evidence.quote: In this context, we aim to provide accurate frequencies of the ground vibrational state of two key aliphatic aldehydes, n-butanal and its branched-chain isomer, i-butanal, to enable their eventual detection in the interstellar medium.
We also want to test the level of complexity that interstellar chemistry can reach in regions of star formation.
This paper makes use of the following ALMA data: ADS/JAO.ALMA#2016.1.00074.S.

analysis_steps.goal: Quantum chemical computations of n- and i-butanal conformers

method.value: Geometry optimization and harmonic vibrational frequency calculations at B2PLYP-D3BJ/aug-cc-pVTZ and CCSD/cc-pVTZ levels, followed by single-point CCSD(T)/CBS energy calculations.

evidence.quote: The geometries were optimized at the density functional theory level, employing the double-hybrid functional B2PLYP (cite: 2006Grimme) combined with Grimme’s D3BJ dispersion (cite: 2011Grimme), in conjunction with the correlation consistent basis set of Dunning aug-cc-pVTZ

Additional optimizations were also carried out using the ab initio coupled-cluster with single and double excitations (CCSD) method (cite: Raghavachari89). In this case the Dunning’s cc-pVTZ (correlation-consistent polarized valence triple-zeta) basis set was employed.

To obtain more accurate stability order, single point calculations were carried out on the CCSD/cc-pVTZ optimized geometries. Energies are calculated at the CCSD(T) (coupled-cluster with single and double excitations including triple excitations through a perturbative treatment) level extrapolated to the complete basis set limit, denoted as CCSD(T)/CBS.

key_parameters.value: n=3 (aug-cc-pVTZ) and n=4 (aug-cc-pVQZ) for CBS extrapolation

evidence.quote: It is computed from the n$^{-3}$ extrapolation equation (cite: Helgaker97) applied to the CCSD(T) energies calculated with the triple- (n=3 aug-cc-pVTZ) and quadruple-zeta (n=4, aug-cc-pVQZ) basis sets.
On the optimized geometries, harmonic vibrational frequencies were calculated at both levels of theory.

validation.value: Confirmed stationary points on the potential energy surface and compared theoretical rotational and centrifugal distortion constants with experimental values.

evidence.quote: This allows the zero-point vibrational energy (ZPE) correction to be estimated, the nature of the stationary points located on the potential energy surface to be confirmed, and the vibrational contribution to the partition function to be computed.

Also, from a comparison between the experimental and theoretically predicted parameters, we can infer that the rotational constants as well as the quartic centrifugal distortion constants are in very good agreement with the CCSD predicted ones.

method.value: Measure room-temperature absorption spectra from 75 to 325 GHz, assign transitions, fit rotational and centrifugal distortion constants using Watson's A-reduced Hamiltonian in the I^r-representation, and compute rotational and vibrational partition functions.

evidence.quote: The room-temperature rotational spectra were recorded separately from 75 to 325 GHz using the millimeter-wave absorption spectrometer at the University of Valladolid (for a detailed description of the instrument, see (cite: Daly14; Alonso16)).

key_parameters.value: Gas pressure ~20 ubar, modulation frequency 10.2 kHz, modulation depth 20-35 kHz, 2f demodulation with 30 ms time constant

evidence.quote: In both experiments, we filled our double-pass free-space glass cell with an optimum gas pressure of about 20 $\mu$bar (no external heating was needed for any of the molecules), which was maintained during the whole course of the experiment.
Also, the output of the synthesizer was frequency modulated at a frequency of 10.2 kHz, with modulation depths varying between 20 to 35 kHz.

After the radiation passed through the cell, the signal was detected using solid-state zero-bias detectors and was sent to a phase-sensitive lock-in amplifier with 2f demodulation (time constant of 30 ms).

(2012). Pickett’s SPFIT/SPCAT program package (Pickett 1991) was used to perform the corresponding fits using a Watson’s A-reduced Hamiltonian in the I$^{r}$-representation (cite: Watson77).

validation.value: Unit-less weighted deviation of the fit close to 1.0 (0.79 to 1.02) and rms deviation < 30 kHz; XIAM predictions confirmed absence of internal rotation splittings.

evidence.quote: No splittings due to internal rotation motion could be observed for either of the conformers, which is in perfect agreement with the computed barrier heights.

Hence, the present experimental data enabled the determination of accurate rotational constants and the full set of quartic and most of the sextic centrifugal distortion constants, showing a remarkable rms deviation of less than 25 kHz for gauche i-PrCHO.

method.value: Extract spectrum toward Sgr B2(N1S), build a population diagram for acetaldehyde across three torsional states to constrain temperature, compute LTE synthetic spectra in Weeds for acetaldehyde and all identified molecules, and derive column density upper limits for propanal and n-/i-butanal.

evidence.quote: To analyze the spectrum of Sgr B2N1S), we produced synthetic spectra under the assumption of local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE) using the software Weeds (cite: Maret11).
We selected the transitions of this molecule that are not too much contaminated by emission or absorption from other species to build a population diagram (Fig. 7).

Assuming that the more complex aldehydes propanal and butanal trace the same region as acetaldehyde, we produced LTE synthetic spectra for these species adopting the same parameters as acetaldehyde with only the column density left as a free parameter.

key_parameters.value: V_sys = 62 km s^-1, emitting size = 2.0'', T_rot = 250 K and 170 K, linewidth = 5.0 km s^-1, V_off = 0.0 km s^-1

evidence.quote: Each species was modeled with a set of five parameters: size of the emitting region ($\theta_{\rm s}$), column density ($N$), temperature ($T_{\rm rot}$), linewidth ($\Delta V$), and velocity offset ($V_{\rm off}$) with respect to the assumed systemic velocity of the source, $V_{\rm sys}=62$ km s$^{-1}$.

Afterward, given that our chemical model suggests that propanal and butanal may trace lower temperatures than acetaldehyde (see Sect. 7), we also computed column density upper limits assuming a temperature of 170 K instead of 250 K.

assumptions.value: LTE assumption justified by high densities; torsional temperature equal to rotational temperature; propanal and butanal trace the same region and physical parameters as acetaldehyde.

findings_qualitative.value: Neither n-butanal nor i-butanal is detected toward Sgr B2(N1S) or G+0.693-0.027; propanal is also not detected toward Sgr B2(N1S).

evidence.quote: We report non-detections of n- and i-butanal toward both sources, Sgr B2(N1S) and G+0.693-0.027.

While propanal is not detected toward Sgr B2(N1S) either, with an abundance at least 5–11 lower than that of acetaldehyde, propanal is found to be 7 times less abundant than acetaldehyde in G+0.693-0.027.

findings_qualitative.value: The family of interstellar aldehydes in the Galactic center region exhibits a drop of approximately one order of magnitude in abundance at each incremental increase in molecular complexity.

evidence.quote: Our astronomical results indicate that the family of interstellar aldehydes in the Galactic center region is characterized by a drop of one order of magnitude in abundance at each incrementation in the level of molecular complexity.
Our results show that with each incremental increase in the size of the alkyl group in the aldehyde molecule, there is a drop of approximately one order of magnitude in abundance.

findings_qualitative.value: Grain-surface chemistry is sufficient to reproduce observed aldehyde ratios in G+0.693-0.027, whereas gas-phase production may play a dominant role in Sgr B2(N1S).

evidence.quote: Grain-surface chemistry appears sufficient to reproduce aldehyde ratios in G+0.693-0.027; gas-phase production may play a more active role in Sgr B2(N1S).
This assumes that gas-phase production of aldehydes is dominant in Sgr B2(N1S), while in G+0.693 aldehyde production on dust grains is sufficient to reproduce observed molecular ratios.

claims.hypothesis: Millimeter-wave rotational spectroscopy of n- and i-butanal up to 325 GHz can provide frequencies accurate enough for confident astronomical searches in the interstellar medium.
claims.experiment: Measured room-temperature absorption spectra of n- and i-butanal from 75 to 325 GHz and fitted rotational and centrifugal distortion constants for their low-energy conformers using Watson's A-reduced Hamiltonian.
claims.result: Assigned over 2800 (cis-gauche) and 1375 (cis-trans) transitions for n-butanal, and 3411 (gauche) and 513 (trans) transitions for i-butanal, achieving fit rms deviations of 25-29 kHz (equivalent radial velocity FWHM < 0.1 km s^-1 at 100 GHz).
claims.finding: The derived spectroscopic parameters and line catalogs are sufficiently accurate and reliable for astronomical searches in hot cores and cold clouds.

evidence.quote: The line catalogs derived from the accurate spectroscopic parameters should be reliable enough for all astronomical observations.

With our experimental data set we can predict the rotational transitions for both isomers with narrow line widths (full width at half maximum, FWHM) of less than 0.1 km s${^{-1}}$ at 100 GHz, expressed in its equivalent radial velocity, which is more than enough to perform a confident astronomical search for these species.

claims.hypothesis: n- and i-butanal are detectable in the gas phase toward the star-forming region Sgr B2(N1S) and the molecular cloud G+0.693-0.027, and their abundances test how aldehyde abundance scales with molecular complexity.
claims.experiment: Searched for n- and i-butanal in the ALMA ReMoCA spectral survey of Sgr B2(N1S) using Weeds LTE models and in the Yebes 40m / IRAM 30m survey of G+0.693-0.027 using MADCUBA-SLIM LTE models, comparing their upper limits to acetaldehyde and propanal.
claims.result: Non-detections of n- and i-butanal in both sources: toward Sgr B2(N1S), propanal, n-butanal, and i-butanal are at least 5-11, 2-6, and 6-18 times less abundant than acetaldehyde; toward G+0.693-0.027, acetaldehyde/propanal is ~7, propanal/ct-n-butanal is >9, and acetaldehyde/ct-n-butanal is >63.
claims.finding: Each incremental step up in alkyl chain length in the aldehyde family leads to an abundance drop of roughly one order of magnitude.

evidence.quote: The acetaldehyde / $s-$propanal ratio is $\sim$7, the $s-$propanal / $ct-n-$butanal ratio is $>$9, and the acetaldehyde / $ct-n-$butanal ratio is $>$ 63 .
Depending on the assumed temperature, we find that propanal, n-butanal, and i-butanal are at least 5–11, 2–6, and 6-18 times less abundant than acetaldehyde, respectively.
Our results show that with each incremental increase in the size of the alkyl group in the aldehyde molecule, there is a drop of approximately one order of magnitude in abundance.

claims.hypothesis: Gas-grain astrochemical models can explain the relative abundances of aldehydes in both hot cores (Sgr B2(N1S)) and shock-heated molecular clouds (G+0.693-0.027).
claims.experiment: Compared the observed aldehyde column density ratios and excitation temperatures in Sgr B2(N1S) and G+0.693-0.027 with the hot-core chemical kinetics model of Garrod et al. (2021) and ice radical abundance proxies.
claims.result: In Sgr B2(N1S), the model reproduces the CH3CHO/CH3OH ratio (~1:30) and high excitation temperature (257 K vs 250 K) via dominant gas-phase CH3CHO production; in G+0.693-0.027, the cold solid-phase CH3CHO/C2H5CHO ratio (~7.7) matches the observed gas-phase ratio (~7) and ice C2H5/C3H7 (~8) matches C2H5CHO/C3H7CHO (>9).
claims.finding: Observational upper limits on propanal and butanal may be close to true abundances if gas-phase production is active in Sgr B2(N1S), while grain-surface production followed by shock sputtering suffices in G+0.693-0.027.

evidence.loc: Discussion: Interstellar chemistry of acetaldehyde, propanal, and butanal
evidence.quote: The models suggest a purely solid-phase ratio of acetaldehyde to propanal of $\sim$7.7. This is in excellent agreement with the observational ratio of $\sim$7.
Finally, our astrochemical models suggest the observational upper limits on both propanal and butanal could be close to their true abundances toward Sgr B2(N1S) and G+0.693.
This assumes that gas-phase production of aldehydes is dominant in Sgr B2(N1S), while in G+0.693 aldehyde production on dust grains is sufficient to reproduce observed molecular ratios.

why_this_data.value: Accurate millimeter-wave laboratory frequencies are mandatory for detecting complex molecules in high-sensitivity spectral surveys such as the ALMA ReMoCA survey of Sgr B2(N) and the IRAM 30m / Yebes 40m survey of G+0.693-0.027; Sgr B2(N1S) was chosen for its lower continuum opacity compared to the main hot core peak.

evidence.quote: Accurate spectroscopic data at high frequencies are usually mandatory for the eventual astronomical detection of many interstellar molecules in several spectral line surveys, such as the EMoCA and ReMoCA surveys conducted with Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) toward Sgr B2(N) (cite: Belloche2017; Belloche2019) and the IRAM 30m survey of the G+0.693-0.027 giant molecular cloud (cite: 2020Rivilla).

This position is offset by about 1$\ensuremath{''}$ to the south of the main hot core Sgr B2(N1) and was chosen by (cite: Belloche19) because of its lower continuum opacity compared to the peak of the hot core.

why_this_method.value: LTE modeling is justified in Sgr B2(N) by the high densities of the hot-core regions, and lower excitation temperatures (170 K in Sgr B2(N1S) and 12 K without vibrational partition function in G+0.693) were adopted to match expected physical and chemical desorption conditions.

evidence.quote: The high densities of the regions where hot-core emission is detected in Sgr B2(N) (cite: Bonfand19) justify this assumption.

Afterward, given that our chemical model suggests that propanal and butanal may trace lower temperatures than acetaldehyde (see Sect. 7), we also computed column density upper limits assuming a temperature of 170 K instead of 250 K.
Since the excitation temperatures of the molecules in G+0.693 are low ($T_{\rm ex}$=5$-$20 K), we did not use the vibrational contribution of the partition function (Q$_v$) in this case.

referee_caveats_inferred: Upper limits in Sgr B2(N1S) are highly sensitive to the assumed rotational temperature because the vibrational partition function rises steeply between 170 K and 250 K.
Severe line confusion in Sgr B2(N1S) means upper limits rely on visual inspection of the least-contaminated channels rather than a formal statistical detection threshold.
Comparisons with astrochemical models for butanal rely on qualitative proxy arguments (ice radical ratios) rather than explicit chemical network integration.

reproducibility.score_reason: The laboratory spectroscopy, partition functions, target coordinates, and LTE model parameters (size, temperature, linewidth, velocity offset, vibrational/conformational correction factors) are thoroughly documented and transition lists are at CDS. However, reproducing the exact astronomical upper limits from scratch requires the custom-reduced ReMoCA spectrum (Melosso et al. 2020), the full background LTE model of all contaminating species in Sgr B2(N1S) and G+0.693-0.027, and the non-ALMA single-dish spectra.
